why: sqrt(16/25)=4/5, 3/9=1/3 and sqrt(196)=14 are all rational, while 5 is not a perfect square so sqrt(5) is irrational.

0.17 terminates and 1.513-recurring and 0.27-46-recurring are non-terminating recurring (hence rational), whereas 0.101001000... has a non-repeating pattern so it is non-terminating non-recurring, i.e. irrational.

Denominators 5, 16=2^4 and 25=5^2 are of the form 2^m*5^n so those expansions terminate (0.4, 0.1875, 5.48), but 11 has a prime factor other than 2 or 5, giving 3/11 = 0.272727... which is non-terminating recurring.
The number line is in one-to-one correspondence with the set of real numbers, so every point on it represents a real number (rationals and irrationals only cover part of it each).
Let x = 0.444...; then 10x = 4.444... so 9x = 4 and x = 4/9 (40/9 and 36/9 exceed 1, and 3.6/9 is not in p/q integer form).
The square root of a natural number is either an integer (when the number is a perfect square) or irrational, so for a non-perfect-square n, sqrt(n) is irrational.
cube-root of 64 simplifies to the rational number 4, so it is not a surd, whereas sqrt(7), cube-root of 17 and sqrt(193) are all irrational roots of rationals.
cube-root of sqrt(5) = (5^(1/2))^(1/3) = 5^(1/6) = sixth root of 5, so the order of the surd is 6.

A conjugate pair is formed by changing the sign of one term so that the product is rational: (2sqrt5+sqrt3)(-2sqrt5+sqrt3) = 3-20 = -17 (rational), while B, C and D all give irrational products; note the more usual form 2sqrt5-sqrt3 is not offered, A being its negative, but A is still the only option forming a genuine conjugate pair.
solution: Two binomial surds form a conjugate pair when their product is a rational number (see "Remember this!" in section 2.4). \((2\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{3})(-2\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{3}) = 3-20 = -17\), which is rational, so option (A) is correct. Options (B), (C) and (D) all give an irrational product. [Note: the conjugate usually written for \(2\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{3}\) is \(2\sqrt{5}-\sqrt{3}\), which is not among the options; option (A) is its negative, and satisfies the same rational-product property.]
